strengths: Simple and practical: one-line modification with minimal overhead, immediately applicable to any momentum-based optimizer
Sound theoretical foundation: Hamiltonian+Descent analysis establishes convergence guarantees and monotonic loss decrease under mild conditions
Broad applicability: demonstrated across AdamW, Lion, and general momentum methods; works without hyperparameter tuning
Comprehensive experiments: scaling studies (60M-1B), multiple domains (language, vision, RLHF), and downstream evaluation on GLUE
Consistent improvements: 1.47× speedup on 1B pretraining, 2% improvement on downstream tasks, robust across different initialization conditions
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale: maximum 1B models with no validation on larger modern scales (7B+); confidence in generalization to production scales is limited
Theory-practice gap: discrete-time theorems only cover single-step improvements with restricted step sizes; no multi-step convergence rate analysis despite multi-step training in practice
Inconsistent optimizer behavior: improvements diverge across optimizers—gap grows for AdamW but shrinks for Lion with model size—mechanism not fully explained

Missing wall-clock time measurements: despite claims of 'virtually no overhead', no actual timing data provided; sparse operations (45-75% of updates masked) may have non-negligible GPU efficiency implications
Modest downstream task improvements: GLUE results show only +1.6 average points with high variance across tasks; no statistical significance testing or error bars reported
Limited baseline comparisons: only compares base vs. cautious variants; no direct empirical comparison to other recent optimizers (Lion, ADOPT, SOAP) on same tasks
Incomplete ablations: no sensitivity analysis for ξ=1 choice or α(x) formula; missing studies on gradient clipping, mixed precision, and small-batch regimes
Incomplete reproducibility: code URL stated as 'available a' is broken; some implementation details relegated to appendix

strengths: Simple and practical one-line modification with potential for wide adoption
Rigorous continuous-time Hamiltonian analysis with clear theoretical framework (Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.2)
Comprehensive experimental scope across LLM pretraining, vision tasks, and downstream evaluation
Clear visualization of optimization trajectories demonstrating monotonic loss decrease
Well-written paper with detailed appendices including pseudocode and hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Element-wise masking by gradient alignment is intuitive but not clearly differentiated from existing gradient clipping, normalization, and conservative update schemes; insufficient engagement with related work

Significant theory-practice gap: Discrete-time Theorem 2.3 requires restrictive, unvalidated step size bounds; Theorem 2.4 uses different mask function than implementation; no convergence rates established for the practical algorithm
Incomplete evaluation: Missing comparisons with recent optimizers (SHAMPOO, SOAP, ADOPT, Schedule-Free); no wall-clock time comparisons (only iteration counts); no error bars or significance testing

Inconsistent and sometimes modest empirical improvements: GLUE results mixed (RTE drops 5.4 points); unexplained asymmetry in scaling across optimizers (AdamW gap increases with model size, Lion decreases); improvements of 3% on downstream tasks

Ad-hoc design choices: Masking function α(x) = dim(x)/(nnz(x>0)+ξ) lacks principled justification; ξ never ablated; no systematic exploration of alternative formulations despite claims of 'new family of optimizers'

Hyperparameter tuning claims undermined: Figure 4 shows effective sparsity changes from 1.0 to 0.55, indicating α(x) significantly alters dynamics despite 'no modification needed' claim; scaling factor acts as hidden hyperparameter
Computational cost understated: Claims 'virtually no overhead' but per-step cardinality computation (∥ϕ_t∥_0) and masking operations incur cost; no GPU wall-clock time analysis provided

Limited applicability analysis: No characterization of when method helps (early vs. late training, loss landscape types); limited transfer value shown in downstream GLUE; missing ablations on step size sensitivity, ϕ function choices, and architecture generalization

strengths: Novel theoretical framework using Hamiltonian mechanics to analyze momentum-based optimizers, with rigorous continuous-time and discrete-time convergence analysis
Exceptionally simple and practical modification requiring only one line of code, with no hyperparameter tuning needed
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple important domains: LLM pretraining (60M-1B), vision (MAE), and post-training tasks (instruction tuning, RLHF)
Consistent improvements demonstrated across different optimizers (AdamW, Lion) and model scales, with 1.47× sample efficiency gain on LLaMA 1B
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, especially the 2D toy example (Section 3.1) demonstrating the intuition behind cautious masking
Strong theoretical insights showing the modification preserves Lyapunov/Hamiltonian functions while accelerating loss decrease
weaknesses: Critical lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or explicit statement of number of runs for any experiments; 1.47× speedup claim lacks uncertainty quantification
Missing comparisons with recent optimizer alternatives (Schedule-Free, SOAP, ADOPT, SHAMPOO) explicitly mentioned in introduction but not empirically evaluated
Suspicious GLUE results (Table 2) with unexplained high volatility: SST2 shows +28% improvement while RTE shows -5% regression, without error analysis or justification
Diminishing improvements at scale: C-AdamW gap shrinks from +0.39 perplexity at 60M to -0.02 at 1B; for Lion at 1B both achieve 21.17, undermining scaling claims
Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2.3 requires restrictive step-size constraints that are never validated against practical settings; multi-step convergence not theoretically guaranteed
Post-training experiments (Section 3.3) are primarily qualitative without statistical testing, significance analysis, or comprehensive baselines beyond AdamW
MAE experiment only compares against single baseline (AdamW); no Lion variant comparison, unclear if single-run result
Mask function design choices not fully justified: α(x) is heuristic; sensitivity to ε parameter not explored; sparsity analysis (Figure 4) limited to single model size
Reproducibility concerns: code availability incomplete ('Code is available a' truncated), unclear number of random seeds, learning rate scaling (Algorithm 2, line 11) is non-standard modification

Discrete-time analysis (Theorem 2.3) only guarantees single-step improvements; gap between single-step and multi-step performance not theoretically bridged, despite acknowledging no-free-lunch constraints

strengths: Simple and practical modification (literally one line) with broad applicability to any momentum-based optimizer, enabling easy adoption
Solid theoretical analysis in both continuous and discrete time using Hamiltonian+Descent framework, with convergence guarantees
Comprehensive experimental validation across LLM pretraining (100M-1.2B models, multiple datasets), image classification, and diverse auxiliary tasks (MAEs, post-training, ablations)
Consistent improvements across diverse optimizers (AdamW, Lion, LaProp, MARS) and tasks, demonstrating robustness of the approach
Good experimental practices including extensive hyperparameter grids, error bars, downstream evaluation, and reproducibility details in appendix
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are modest (0.1-1.5% on main tasks) with several results <0.5%, lacking statistical significance testing despite small effect sizes
Core novelty is limited—gradient alignment concepts are well-established; the contribution is primarily an engineering insight rather than fundamental algorithmic advance
Central claim about 'minimum hyperparameter tuning' is contradicted by Table 5, showing C-AdamW requires different optimal β₁, β₂, and ε values than AdamW
3% throughput reduction is non-negligible given modest improvements; additional communication overhead in distributed settings under-discussed

Theory-practice gap: discrete-time results (Theorems 2.3-2.4) require restricted step sizes or specific masks; inner-product mask provably helps only on convex functions while element-wise mask (used in practice) helps under restricted conditions
Downstream task evaluation shows mixed results (5/7 improved, 2 regressed including PIQA and Lambada), questioning universal applicability
No empirical comparison with other recent optimizer alternatives (Schedule-Free, SOAP, ADOPT) mentioned in introduction despite claiming better results
Masking ~45% of dimensions on average (Fig 4) without discussing potential negative consequences for sparse/structured problems or analyzing failure modes

strengths: Simple and general modification applicable to any momentum-based optimizer
Technically sound continuous-time theoretical analysis using Hamiltonian dynamics framework
Comprehensive experiments across LLM pretraining, image classification, and multiple model scales
Consistent (though marginal) improvements across different optimizers and tasks
Clear presentation of methods and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are marginal (0.1-1%) and lack statistical significance testing; insufficient for a top-tier venue
Key claims contradicted by experimental details: claims 'minimum hyperparameter tuning' despite extensive coordinate-descent search with different hyperparameters across scales (Table 5)

Severe theory-practice gap: discrete-time theorems have impractical step-size constraints; continuous-time analysis doesn't transfer to practice; authors acknowledge extending to multiple steps is 'challenging'
The 55% sparsity ratio from masking (Figure 4) is concerning and inadequately analyzed; unclear if gains come from optimization or implicit regularization
Limited novelty: sign-alignment masking is straightforward; Hamiltonian analysis doesn't provide surprising insights into why momentum optimization fails
Unfair experimental comparison: C-AdamW received extensive grid search while baselines appear to use standard hyperparameters; makes it impossible to isolate contribution of cautious masking
Missing comparisons with other recent optimizers (SOAP, SHAMPOO, Schedule-Free, ADOPT) mentioned in introduction
Computational overhead of ~3% (Table 9) partially offsets reported improvements; unclear if net benefit exists when accounting for tuning costs
Sparse analysis of when and why the method works; no failure cases discussed; missing ablations on design choices like ξ=1

strengths: Genuine simplicity and practicality: single-line modification applicable to any momentum-based optimizer without complex tuning
Rigorous theoretical framework using Hamiltonian mechanics with proofs for both continuous and discrete time cases
Comprehensive experimental validation across LLM pretraining (multiple scales), image classification, MAE pretraining, instruction tuning, and RLHF
Excellent reproducibility with detailed pseudocode, hyperparameter grids, and extensive appendix
Consistent improvements across diverse settings and multiple base optimizers (AdamW, Lion, LaProp, MARS, Muon)
Strong presentation with intuitive 2D toy example and thorough ablation studies on mask functions
weaknesses: Modest magnitude of improvements: LLM pretraining gains average ~0.3-1.0%, downstream task improvements within typical variance ranges and not statistically significant
Computational overhead of 3% throughput reduction (571.8k → 560.5k tokens/s) contradicts claims of negligible cost, potentially offsetting perplexity gains in wall-clock time
Theory-practice gap: Theorems 2.3-2.4 require data-dependent step size conditions difficult to verify in practice; continuous-time analysis doesn't directly justify discrete stochastic improvements

Confounding experimental design: optimal C-AdamW uses different β₁ values (0.95-0.98 vs 0.9) than baseline AdamW, making attribution unclear; claims 'without hyperparameter modification' contradicted by extensive search
Missing statistical rigor: single runs reported without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; downstream results (Table 3) have margins within noise (~0.5%)
Limited novelty: element-wise alignment masking is relatively straightforward; scaling factor α(x) design appears arbitrary without justification
Inconsistent results unexplored: C-Lion tolerates higher learning rates than Lion; improvements vary from 0.1% to 1% across scales with unclear root causes

Incomplete analysis: no systematic study of failure modes, limited ablation on design choices (scaling factor ε, alignment threshold), insufficient baseline comparisons with recent optimizer alternatives
